1. Liver Anatomy and Physiology Review

  • The liver filters toxins and waste from the bloodstream and produces bile, secreted into the small intestine to aid digestion. Hepatocytes also process nutrients.
VesselDirection and content
Hepatic arteryCirculation → liver: oxygenated blood
Portal veinGI tract → liver: nutrient-rich blood
Hepatic veinLiver → circulation: filtered blood (via the sinusoids and central vein)
Bile ductLiver → gallbladder (stored) or small intestine
  • Both arterial and portal blood pass through the sinusoidal capillaries, where molecules are exchanged with hepatocytes; filtered blood exits via the central vein into the hepatic vein.
Liver anatomy and the hepatic lobule (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

2. Liver Failure: Acute vs Chronic

Her summary tableThe bolded red items in her table below are the highest yield.
Acute liver failureChronic liver failure
DefinitionRapid-onset liver failure (sudden, massive hepatic destruction; within 26 weeks of initial injury)Long-term, progressive liver failure (months-years)
PathogenesisDirect liver damage (acetaminophen, other toxins); direct damage plus inflammation (hepatitis)Chronic hepatocyte injury (hepatitis, steatotic liver disease) → inflammation and fibrosis → cirrhosis
MorphologyMicro: massive/confluent hepatic necrosis
Gross: shrunken, soft, yellow, often not fibrotic		Micro: bridging necrosis, regenerative nodules
Gross: extensive fibrosis, nodular, firm
ComplicationsHepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, cholestasis, hypoglycemia, nausea/vomitingPortal hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, encephalopathy, cholestasis, HCC risk

Acute liver failure

  • Causes: acetaminophen overdose (most common, ~50% of US cases), other toxins, autoimmune hepatitis, viral hepatitis (A and B take longer, because damage is direct viral toxicity plus the inflammatory response).

Acetaminophen toxicity

  1. Most acetaminophen is conjugated by glucuronidation and sulfation into a nontoxic metabolite excreted in urine.
  2. Some is metabolized by CYP2E1 into the toxic metabolite NAPQI (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction), normally detoxified with glutathione.
  3. In overdose the normal pathways are overwhelmed, more goes to NAPQI, glutathione is depleted, NAPQI accumulates → centrilobular necrosis → liver failure.
  4. Failure comes ~1 week after onset of jaundice: fulminant liver failure.

Morphology

  • Gross: shrunken, soft, with specks of yellow necrosis; no scarring (disease moves too fast for inflammation and fibrosis).
  • Micro: confluent necrosis across a large area (vs focal necrosis): eosinophilic with loss of cellular structure, compared with normal parenchyma.
Acute liver failure: gross and confluent necrosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Complications of acute failure

  • Hepatic encephalopathy: failure to remove toxins, especially ammonia → confusion, asterixis, coma, death. Also occurs in Reye syndrome (children after aspirin).
  • Coagulopathy: impaired synthesis of clotting factors (prothrombin, fibrinogen) → easy bruising and poorly controlled bleeding.
  • Hepatorenal syndrome: mechanism not fully known; reduced kidney perfusion → decreased urine output and kidney failure without other kidney injury.
  • Also nausea/vomiting, cholestasis/jaundice, hypoglycemia.

Chronic liver failure and cirrhosis

  • Most associated with cirrhosis (extensive fibrosis and remodeling), although cirrhosis can exist without chronic failure and chronic failure without cirrhosis. Causes: chronic viral hepatitis, alcohol-associated and metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, others.
  • Mechanism: chronic hepatocyte injury → recruitment of Kupffer cells and stellate cells → signaling, especially TGF-β → stellate cells differentiate into activated myofibroblasts → deposit extracellular matrix (collagen) → repeated → bridging fibrosis separating parenchyma into regenerative nodules.
  • Fibrosis vs cirrhosis: fibrosis = collagen deposition after injury; cirrhosis = diffuse bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules and architectural distortion.
  • Gross: firm, fibrotic, nodular. Micro: architecture distorted; trichrome stain highlights collagen; bridging fibrosis from bridging necrosis; inflammation is variable (not a key feature).
Cirrhosis: regenerative nodules and bridging fibrosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Complications of chronic failure

  • Anorexia, weakness, cholestasis/jaundice, hyperestrogenemia, hepatic encephalopathy, HCC, portal hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome.
  • Portal hypertension: increased portal vein pressure and vascular resistance → diminished perfusion into the liver. Causes: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis most common; schistosomiasis, congenital hepatic fibrosis), posthepatic (Budd-Chiari, right-sided heart failure, constrictive pericarditis). Complications: ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, splenomegaly, portosystemic shunts (esophageal varices, caput medusae).
  • Hepatopulmonary syndrome: right-to-left shunting from dilated pulmonary capillaries and precapillary vessels → V/Q mismatch (venous blood bypasses alveoli) → hypoxemia and dyspnea.
Portal hypertension pathophysiology and complications (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Hepatopulmonary syndrome (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

3. Autoimmune Hepatitis

  • Progressive chronic autoimmune disease with autoantibodies, triggered by viral infection, toxins or vaccination. Female predominance (~78%); associated with certain HLA alleles. Features range from fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain to cirrhosis and death. Can also cause acute liver failure.

Morphology

  • Interface hepatitis: CD4+ helper T cells and plasma cells infiltrate the junction between the portal tract and parenchyma, driving necrosis and damage.
  • Emperipolesis: lymphocytes/plasma cells within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes.
  • Rosettes of regenerating hepatocytes forming in response to periportal necrosis.
Autoimmune hepatitis: interface hepatitis, emperipolesis, rosettes (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Four diagnostic criteria

  1. Autoantibodies (no single one; type 1 vs type 2)
  2. Elevated serum IgG
  3. Exclusion of viral hepatitis
  4. Histologic findings (above)
TypePopulationAutoantibodies
Type 1More common overall; adultsANA, anti-smooth muscle actin (ASMA) (the two most common); soluble liver antigen/liver-pancreas antigen (SLA/LP); antimitochondrial (AMA)
Type 2ChildrenAnti-liver kidney microsome-1 (LKM-1); anti-liver cytosol-1 (LC-1)
  • Antibody titers do not indicate disease severity (unlike, e.g., vasculitis in CV II).
Autoimmune hepatitis diagnostic criteria and antibodies (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

4. Steatotic Liver Disease: Alcohol-Associated vs MASLD

Alcohol-associated liver disease

  • Accumulation of fat in the liver from excess alcohol exposure. Reference thresholds (context, not for memorization): 80 g alcohol (~6 beers) over one to several days = mild, reversible steatosis; 80 g daily = significant risk; 160 g daily over 10-20+ years = severe injury.

Alcohol metabolism

  1. Ethanol → acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) in the cytoplasm, using NAD+ (→ NADH).
  2. Acetaldehyde → acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase in the mitochondria.
  3. Acetate → acetyl-CoA (master metabolite) → includes triglyceride synthesis.
  4. Minor pathway: CYP2E1 converts ethanol to acetaldehyde and generates reactive oxygen species.

Three pathogenic mechanisms

  1. ↓ Fatty acid oxidation: ADH use of NAD+ → depleted NAD+ and ↑ NADH (imbalanced NADH:NAD+ ratio) → ↓ β-oxidation → fatty acids build up.
  2. ↑ Triglyceride synthesis and accumulation: ↑ acetaldehyde, acetate, acetyl-CoA → more triglyceride.
  3. ↑ ROS generation: CYP2E1 pathway → direct hepatocyte damage.
Alcohol metabolism and three mechanisms (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Progression

StageFeatures
Steatosis (fatty liver)Gross: enlarged, soft, yellow. Micro: lipid droplets, here macrovesicular steatosis (can be microvesicular).
Steatohepatitis (continued use or binge in a healthy liver)↑ oxidative stress from ROS plus inflammation. Neutrophil infiltrate; ballooned hepatocytes (enlarged, clear grainy cytoplasm: severe cell distress); Mallory-Denk bodies (bright pink eosinophilic inclusions of degraded keratin from cytoskeletal damage); chicken-wire pericellular fibrosis (Sirius red).
CirrhosisMicronodular (nodules ~3 mm), bridging fibrosis, regenerative nodules; ↑ risk of HCC.
  • Damage is reversible with abstinence up to this point; at cirrhosis it becomes irreversible.
Alcohol-associated steatosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Steatohepatitis: ballooned hepatocytes, neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies, chicken-wire fibrosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Micronodular cirrhosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)

  • Formerly NAFLD; renamed to reflect the mechanism. Fat accumulation from metabolic dysfunction, most strongly associated with insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia.
  • Mechanism: insulin resistance impairs regulation of adipose lipolysis → ↑ free fatty acids to organs including the liver → triglyceride accumulation and lipotoxicity (ER stress, mitochondrial dysfunction) → ↑ oxidative stress, inflammation, damage.
  • Progression: healthy → MASLD → MASH (steatohepatitis) → cirrhosis → HCC.
  • Morphology is similar to alcohol: macrovesicular steatosis, ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies, chicken-wire fibrosis; "lobular inflammation" with possibly fewer neutrophils.
  • Differentiate by cause and labs: AST > ALT (about 2:1) with alcohol; AST < ALT in early MASLD (can change with progression).
MASLD morphology and differentiators (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Alcohol-associatedMASLD/MASH
DefinitionFat accumulation due to excess alcohol exposureFat accumulation due to metabolic dysfunction without significant alcohol exposure
PathogenesisAlcohol and metabolic byproducts create redox imbalance favoring fat storage and lipogenesisMultiple mechanisms driven by insulin resistance, obesity, diabetes
MorphologyGross: enlarged, soft, yellow, greasy. Micro: lipid droplets, ballooned hepatocytes, neutrophil infiltrates, Mallory-Denk bodies, chicken-wire fibrosisSimilar; "lobular inflammation" with possibly fewer neutrophils
ComplicationsSteatohepatitis → cirrhosis → liver failure or HCCMASH → cirrhosis → liver failure or HCC

Stages and manifestations of alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD)

ALD is a spectrum of liver injury caused by chronic, excessive alcohol consumption. It is the most common cause of liver disease in the West.

PathophysiologyExcess alcohol metabolism increases NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) production, causing decreased fatty acid oxidation and increased lipogenesis
Location of initial injuryDamage, steatosis and fibrosis typically begin in Zone III of the liver acinus (centrilobular)
Key lab markerElevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) is a sensitive indicator of alcohol use
Stage / conditionKey featuresHistology / microscopic findingsClinical and lab findingsPrognosis
Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver)The liver becomes heavy and greasy due to fat accumulationMacrovesicular fatty change: large fat droplets displace the hepatocyte nucleus to the peripheryOften asymptomatic; may have mild elevation in liver enzymesReversible with abstinence is possible
Alcoholic hepatitisAcute or chronic inflammatory condition driven by acetaldehyde toxicity (also responsible for “hangover” nausea and headache); cytokine release (e.g., interleukin-8) attracts neutrophilsSwollen (ballooning) and necrotic hepatocytes with neutrophilic infiltration; Mallory bodies (eosinophilic inclusions of damaged keratin filaments). Mallory bodies are not specific: they also occur in other conditions such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH)Painful hepatomegaly; AST > ALT (ratio > 2:1); both unconjugated and conjugated hyperbilirubinemiaCan resolve, but repeated episodes significantly accelerate progression to cirrhosis
Alcoholic cirrhosisFinal stage of liver injury, leading to portal hypertension and end-stage liver diseaseEarly: sclerosis (fibrosis) around the central vein. Advanced: regenerative nodules separated by thick bands of fibrosis, destroying the normal liver architectureSigns of liver failure (jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy); portal hypertension (varices)Usually irreversible

AST = aspartate aminotransferase; ALT = alanine aminotransferase. Progression is not guaranteed: features can co-exist and dominate at different times.

5. Inherited Liver Disease: Hemochromatosis, Wilson Disease, A1AT Deficiency

Hemochromatosis

  • Excess iron absorption: normal body iron 2-6 g; hemochromatosis >50 g. The liver regulates iron absorption through hepcidin; reduced hepcidin → increased intestinal iron absorption.
  • Hereditary (mutations reducing hepcidin synthesis): adult: HAMP, HFE, TfR2, ferroportin; juvenile: HJV. Secondary (hemosiderosis): iron overload from regular transfusions, increased oral intake, chronic liver disease.
  • Most common at 40-50 years in males; females counterbalance with menstruation (and pregnancy), presenting later if at all.
  • Gross: enlarged liver with dark brown discoloration. Micro: hemosiderin (golden-yellow on H&E; blue on Prussian blue).
  • Presentation triad: micronodular cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, abnormal skin pigmentation.
  • Systemic: atrophied fibrotic pancreas, enlarged heart with hemosiderosis, acute synovitis and pseudogout, small atrophic testes. 200× greater risk of HCC.
Hemochromatosis: gross, hemosiderin H&E and Prussian blue (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Wilson disease

  • ATP7B mutation: impaired copper secretion into bile and impaired incorporation into apoceruloplasmin to form ceruloplasmin → ↑ free copper (toxic: generates ROS).
  • Morphology: steatosis → cirrhosis. Copper staining is not sensitive or specific (unlike iron staining in hemochromatosis).
  • Neurologic: copper accumulates in the basal ganglia and cornea: movement disorder, psychiatric symptoms, Kayser-Fleischer rings (brown rings around the iris).
Wilson disease (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

A1AT (α1-antitrypsin) deficiency

  • A protein-folding disease with low circulating A1AT, a glycoprotein protease inhibitor that inhibits neutrophil elastase at inflammation sites. Polymorphic gene: PiMM is the most common genotype; PiZZ is the most aberrant (most strongly associated with deficiency).
  • The mutant polypeptide misfolds and aggregates in the ER → ER stress and injury.
  • Micro: dark purple PAS-positive globules of accumulated glycoprotein.
  • Liver: hepatitis, cirrhosis, HCC. Most often it causes pulmonary emphysema (unregulated neutrophil elastase in the lung).
A1AT deficiency: PAS globules (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
DiseaseLiverExtrahepatic
HemochromatosisCirrhosis, HCCDiabetes, skin pigmentation, cardiomyopathy
WilsonSteatosis, cirrhosisNeurologic/psychiatric, Kayser-Fleischer rings
A1ATHepatitis, cirrhosis, HCCPulmonary emphysema

6. Circulatory Disorders of the Liver

Anything impairing blood flow into, within or out of the liver.

SiteDisorderNotes
IntoHepatic artery compromiseEmboli, thrombi, compression → liver infarct (artery delivers oxygen)
IntoPortal vein obstructionThrombosis, infection, trauma, malignancy, inflammation
WithinIntrahepatic obstructionCirrhosis (most common), sickle cell disease (misshapen cells stuck in vasculature), eclampsia, malignancy
OutSinusoidal obstruction syndromeSinusoidal epithelial injury after chemotherapy or allogeneic stem cell transplant; obstruction/obliteration of sinusoids, extensive congestion, hepatocyte necrosis
OutBudd-Chiari syndromeHepatic vein thrombosis; hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, ascites; hemorrhagic necrosis
OutPassive congestionRight-sided heart failure → chronic hepatic congestion: "nutmeg liver" grossly, centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis microscopically
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and Budd-Chiari (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Nutmeg liver and centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

7. Bilirubin Metabolism and Cholestatic Disease

Bilirubin biochemistry

  • Bile = bilirubin, bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids.
  1. Old red cells are broken down by macrophages (spleen); heme → unconjugated bilirubin (toxic, insoluble).
  2. Binds albumin in the blood and travels to the liver.
  3. Hepatocytes take it up and use UGT1A1 in the endoplasmic reticulum to conjugate it to glucuronic acid → conjugated bilirubin (soluble, nontoxic).
  4. Excreted into bile → intestine, where bacteria convert it to urobilinogen: most is excreted in feces (stercobilin), some is reabsorbed and recycled to the liver (enterohepatic circulation) or excreted in urine (urobilin).
Bilirubin biochemistry (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Cholestasis

  • Impeded flow of bile from the liver to the intestine → backup of bile components (bilirubin, bile salts) → hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice (yellow pigment in skin and eyes).
  • Micro: green-brown bile accumulation in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells and in dilated canaliculi (bile plugs); bile salt accumulation in hepatocytes gives a swollen, foamy feathery degeneration.
Bile plug and feathery degeneration (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Causes

Physiologic jaundice of the newborn

  • Low UGT1A1 at birth → reduced conjugation → backup of insoluble unconjugated bilirubin. UGT1A1 rises naturally by ~3-4 months.
  • Treatment: blue light phototherapy converts bilirubin into a soluble isomer for excretion.

Hereditary hyperbilirubinemia

TypeSyndromeDefect
UnconjugatedCrigler-Najjar type 1UGT1A1 complete loss of function; unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses into the brain → kernicterus, fatal
Crigler-Najjar type 2UGT1A1 partial loss of function (much less severe)
Gilbert syndromeUGT1A1 transient impairment of function (mild)
ConjugatedDubin-Johnson syndromeMRP2 gene mutation (defective bilirubin excretion from hepatocytes) → darkening of hepatocytes
Rotor syndromeDefective storage of bilirubin in the liver
Hereditary hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Large bile duct obstruction

  • Adults: choledocholithiasis (stones in the extrahepatic duct), pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Children: biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis, choledochal cysts.
  • Morphology: edema in the portal tract and neutrophils at the portal tract-parenchyma interface = pericholangitis.
Large duct obstruction: pericholangitis and edema (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Sepsis

  • Cholestasis from circulating infection, direct infection, or ischemia after sepsis-driven hypotension. Ductal cholestasis: dense bile plugs in dilated canals of Hering and ductules at the portal-parenchymal interface.
Ductal cholestasis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Primary hepatolithiasis

  • Stones within the intrahepatic bile ducts; block ducts and damage parenchyma. Also called recurrent pyogenic cholangitis (association with chronic bacterial or parasitic infection); high prevalence in East Asia. Visible on CT.
Primary hepatolithiasis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Neonatal cholestasis (jaundice longer than expected)

  • Biliary atresia: complete or partial obstruction of the bile duct (congenital abnormality or other occlusion) → congestion, parenchymal damage, bridging fibrosis and bile plugs → early cirrhosis at 3-6 months.
  • Nonobstructive neonatal cholestasis: Alagille syndrome (genetic defect impairing biliary tree development), inborn errors of metabolism, neonatal hepatitis (infection or inherited disease; multinucleated giant hepatocytes, canalicular bile plugs).
Biliary atresia and nonobstructive neonatal cholestasis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Autoimmune cholangiopathies

  • PBC and PSC (next section).

8. Primary Biliary Cholangitis, Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis and Ascending Cholangitis

PBCPSC
DefinitionAutoimmune disease of the small-medium sized intrahepatic bile ducts (destruction)Autoimmune disease of the large bile ducts (intrahepatic or extrahepatic); obliterative fibrosis
PathogenesisT cells and antimitochondrial antibodies (AMAs) against PDC-E2 (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex E2); middle-aged womenT cells and autoantibodies against MHC alleles; trigger environmental and genetic; associated with ulcerative colitis; middle-aged men; MPO-ANCA in 65%
MorphologyFlorid duct lesion: destructive granulomatous inflammation around a bile duct; late: feathery degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodiesOnion-skin concentric periductal fibrosis; strictures (luminal narrowing) show as beading on radiography
Clinical / labsAsymptomatic or fatigue; hypercholesterolemia; ↑ ALP, IgM, AMA (95%); → jaundice, splenomegaly, cirrhosisFatigue, jaundice, pancreatic involvement, cirrhosis; no specific autoantibody
ComplicationsCirrhosis, HCCCirrhosis, cholangiocarcinoma (~20% risk)
PBC: florid duct lesion (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
PSC: onion-skin fibrosis and beading (red arrows = dilation, white arrows = strictures) (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Primary cholangitis: PBC vs PSC at a glance

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
GenderMore common among middle-aged womenMore common among middle-aged men
PathophysiologyProgressive autoimmune destruction of only intrahepatic small and medium-sized bile ductsProgressive chronic inflammation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts
Clinical presentationFatigue, progressive symptoms of cholestasis (e.g., jaundice, pruritus), hepatosplenomegaly; advanced disease: liver cirrhosis
Potentially dyslipidemias: xanthomas and xanthelasmaCan present with acute cholangitis (fever, chills, right upper quadrant pain)
AntibodiesAnti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA)p-ANCA (perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody)
Laboratory tests↑ ALP, ↑ GGT, and ↑ conjugated bilirubin
Associated conditionsAutoimmune conditions (e.g., sicca syndrome); osteoporosisUlcerative colitis; cholangiocarcinoma
Most accurate diagnostic testLiver biopsy: lymphocytic infiltration of portal areas and periductal granulomasMRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography): multifocal bile duct strictures and dilatations (beading)
ManagementFirst line: ursodeoxycholic acid; liver transplantation is a must if cirrhosis is advancedSupportive; can give ursodeoxycholic acid; interventional treatment: ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography)

ALP = alkaline phosphatase; GGT = gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase.

Ascending (acute) cholangitis

  • Obstruction of the extrahepatic bile duct with infection; can progress to a hepatic abscess.
  • Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain.
  • Can occur with PSC or biliary atresia. A stone obstructing the common bile duct can lead to ascending cholangitis.

9. Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis

Cholelithiasis (gallstones)

  • 95% of biliary tract disease; >20 million people in the US at any time. Risk: middle to older age, female (estrogen: oral contraceptives, pregnancy), gallbladder stasis, genetic predisposition.
  • Clinical: asymptomatic or excruciating right upper quadrant pain; obstruction and inflammation; gallstone pancreatitis (stone obstructs the ampulla/pancreatic duct).
  • Location terms: cholelithiasis = gallbladder; hepatolithiasis = within the liver; choledocholithiasis = bile duct outside the liver.
Gallstone locations (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Cholesterol stonesPigment stones
Pathogenesis(1) Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol; (2) gallbladder stasis; (3) accelerated cholesterol crystallization (nucleation); (4) increased mucus secretion (traps crystals)Unconjugated bilirubin as the primary component; hemolytic anemia (e.g. sickle cell), biliary infection
MorphologyPale yellow, round, hard; 50-100% cholesterol crystals; often multiple small stones, sometimes one or two largeBrown (mixed) stones: infection (e.g. E. coli), some cholesterol, soft and greasy. Black stones: sterile, calcium salts + unconjugated bilirubin, numerous and friable
ImagingRadiolucent if mostly cholesterol; radiopaque if 10-20% calcium carbonateBrown: radiolucent. Black: radiopaque (calcium)
Cholesterol stones (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Pigment stones (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Acute cholecystitis

  • Short-term inflammation of the gallbladder. Calculous (gallstone obstruction, 90%) vs acalculous (ischemia from another condition, ~10%).
  • Gross: enlarged, tense, discolored; red = subserosal hemorrhages; green-black = gangrenous; pus-like exudate on the serosa = empyema.
  • Clinical features follow gallstones; most patients do not have jaundice. Possible complications: hemorrhage, gangrene, abscess, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis.
Acute cholecystitis: normal, hemorrhage, empyema, gangrenous (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Chronic cholecystitis

  • Long-term inflammation, often from recurrent acute cholecystitis; >90% associated with gallstones. Morphology highly variable:
  • Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses: outpouchings of mucosal epithelium into the wall; thickened wall; mononuclear (lymphocytic) infiltrates.
  • Porcelain gallbladder: extensive calcification (seen on radiography).
  • Hyalinizing cholecystitis: dense fibrosis of the wall and mucosa; increased cancer risk.
Chronic cholecystitis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

10. Study Guide Key: Guiding Questions and Image Matching

Dr. McCuen's study guide questions that match the lectures, answers collapsed. Try each first.

Liver failure

Why can acetaminophen cause rapid liver failure?NAPQI is normally detoxified by glutathione; in overdose glutathione is depleted and NAPQI accumulates, causing massive centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis.
Fibrosis vs cirrhosis?Fibrosis is collagen deposition after chronic injury. Cirrhosis is diffuse bridging fibrosis separating regenerative nodules, with architectural distortion and impaired function.
How does hepatocyte injury become cirrhosis?Chronic hepatocyte injury → inflammation → stellate cell activation → collagen deposition → bridging fibrosis → regenerative nodules.

Autoimmune hepatitis

Characteristic histologic features?Interface hepatitis, CD4+ T cells and plasma cells, emperipolesis, rosettes of regenerating hepatocytes.
How can it lead to acute liver failure vs cirrhosis?Severe immune-mediated injury gives massive necrosis and acute failure; persistent inflammation and healing activate stellate cells, producing fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Steatotic liver disease

Mechanisms by which alcohol causes lipid accumulation?ADH-driven NAD+/NADH imbalance reduces fatty acid oxidation; ethanol metabolism directly increases triglyceride synthesis; (also impaired lipoprotein export, etc.).
Alcohol vs MASLD lipid accumulation?Alcohol: driven by ethanol metabolism. MASLD: driven by insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction.

Inherited liver disease

Why does a liver mutation raise systemic iron?The liver regulates iron through hepcidin; defective regulation increases intestinal absorption.
Why is hemochromatosis more prevalent in males?Females lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy, delaying accumulation.
Why is free copper toxic but ceruloplasmin-bound copper not?Free copper participates in oxidative reactions that generate ROS and injury; ceruloplasmin safely binds and transports it.
Why is iron staining useful but copper staining not?Iron forms visible deposits that stain with Prussian blue; copper is diffusely distributed and hard to detect by routine stains.

Circulatory

Causes of impaired pre-, intra- and posthepatic flow?Prehepatic: hepatic artery or portal vein thrombosis/embolism, compression. Intrahepatic: cirrhosis, sickle cell, eclampsia, malignancy. Posthepatic: Budd-Chiari, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, right-sided heart failure.

Bile duct and gallbladder

Why does excess bilirubin turn the skin and eyes yellow?Bilirubin is a yellow pigment that accumulates in elastin-rich tissues (sclera, skin).
PBC vs PSC differences?PBC: florid duct lesion, small intrahepatic ducts, AMA, women, other autoimmune diseases. PSC: onion-skin fibrosis, large intra- and extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA, men, ulcerative colitis.
Why do stones form in the gallbladder (and kidneys, bladder)?Supersaturation, stasis in organs that store or transport fluid, and nucleation of crystallization.
How can a gallstone cause cholecystitis, pancreatitis, ascending cholangitis?Cystic duct obstruction → cholecystitis; ampulla of Vater obstruction → pancreatitis; common bile duct obstruction → bacterial infection (ascending cholangitis).
